status: DRAFT v0.1: not yet reviewed, pretested or calibrated.
notes: Written about principles and amounts, with no current-administration context, because trade positions realigned recently and current-policy wording would cue party.

items.stem: Which comes closest to your view of tariffs, the taxes the US charges on imported goods?
items.scope: Think about trade policy in general, not one country.
options: Few or no tariffs; free trade benefits most people
Low tariffs, used mainly against countries that break trade rules
Moderate tariffs on many goods to protect key US industries
High tariffs on most imports to bring manufacturing back, even if prices rise

items.stem: Would you support tariffs that protect US factory jobs if they raised prices of goods like cars and appliances by about 10%?
items.scope: Assume both effects happen: more factory jobs and higher prices.
options: No; lower prices matter more
Only if prices rose much less, around 2% to 3%
Yes; protecting those jobs is worth it

items.stem: Who should decide how high tariffs are?
items.scope: Answer for any president of either party.
options: Congress only, by passing laws
Congress, but the president can add tariffs in a true emergency
The president, whenever the president judges it's in the national interest

items.stem: Should the US sign more agreements with other countries to lower tariffs on both sides?
items.scope: Agreements that lower trade barriers for both countries.
options: Yes, with as many countries as possible
Yes, but only with strong labor and environmental rules
Only with close allies
No; pull out of existing ones where possible

items.stem: Should the US make trade deals that open foreign markets to US companies if some US industries lose jobs to imports?
items.scope: Assume the country as a whole gains, but some regions lose jobs.
options: Yes; the overall gains outweigh the losses
Yes, but only with major help for workers who lose jobs
No; protecting existing US jobs comes first

items.stem: How much should the US limit trade with China?
options: Trade freely, as with other countries
Limit only sensitive technology, like advanced chips and military goods
Also move production of essentials, like medicines and electronics, out of China
Cut off most trade with China

items.stem: Should companies based in China be allowed to own US businesses, farmland or apps?
items.scope: Companies headquartered in China, whether privately or state-owned.
options: Yes, like any foreign company
Yes, except in sensitive areas like defense and personal data
No farmland, key technology or popular apps; other businesses are fine
No; ban Chinese ownership of US businesses entirely

items.stem: Should the government pay companies to build factories in specific industries in the US, such as computer chips and batteries?
items.scope: Subsidies and tax credits for particular industries.
options: Yes, in many industries
Only in industries vital to national security
No; the market should decide where investment goes
items.notes: Expected to cross-cut: some who favor tariffs oppose subsidies and vice versa. High pole is 'less intervention', the opposite direction from tariff_level.

items.stem: Should federal agencies be required to buy American-made goods, even if they cost more?
items.scope: Everyday government purchases, like vehicles, steel and equipment.
options: No; buy the best value
Only for military and security needs
Yes, if they cost no more than about 25% extra
Yes, always, even at much higher cost

items.stem: Should companies that move US jobs to other countries face penalties?
items.scope: Companies closing US operations and moving that work abroad.
options: Yes, such as higher taxes and losing government contracts
No penalty, but end any tax breaks that make moving jobs abroad cheaper
No; companies should decide where to operate
